suggestions.title: Harakiri
suggestions.description: The highest-rated film on your entire list that has never been shown: 8.6, and no round has ever picked it. This is the anti-samurai samurai film, written by Shinobu Hashimoto - the screenwriter of Seven Samurai, already on your list, and of Rashomon - and directed by Masaki Kobayashi, who answers Kurosawa's heroic code with a courtroom of hypocrisy. Tatsuya Nakadai plays Tsugumo Hanshiro, an unemployed ronin who walks into the courtyard of the House of Iyi and asks permission to commit seppuku on the premises. The clan, embarrassed and expecting a bluff, tells him the story of the last ronin who came begging - and then he tells them his. The structure is a slow unfolding of one debt of honour after another, and the whole film pays off in a windblown duel in a field where the choreography is deliberately ugly rather than beautiful. Toru Takemitsu's score is sparse percussion and silence. It won the Special Jury Prize at Cannes in 1963 and remains the most wounding argument ever made on film that a code of honour is a machine for killing poor men. If Seven Samurai is the template, this is the indictment.

suggestions.title: Modern Times
suggestions.description: Your list has Metropolis (1927) on it, which is the machine age as dread - and it has no answer to that, and no Chaplin at all. Modern Times is the reply: the machine age as slapstick, made nine years later with the same machinery, and it is the oldest comedy on your entire list. Chaplin wrote, directed, produced, scored and starred, and refused to go talkie even in 1936 - the film is silent except for synchronized sound effects and one gag of pure genius, the factory feeding machine that force-feeds a man his lunch at high speed. The opening image of the Tramp on the assembly line, tightening bolts until his arms twitch convulsively in his sleep, is the most quoted image in the history of film comedy. Paulette Goddard plays the gamin, an orphan who survives by stealing bananas; their partnership is the warmth the film runs on, and the ending - she and the Tramp walking off down an empty road toward the horizon - is the template every optimistic ending since has borrowed. Chaplin's own voice appears on screen for the first time in the nonsense song - the only dialogue-like sound in a 1936 film that refuses to talk. Eighty-seven minutes, and not a wasted shot.

suggestions.title: Dune: Part One
suggestions.description: Your list of 99 films has nothing on it from the 2020s, and this is the decade's most ambitious piece of large-scale filmmaking. Denis Villeneuve is already on your list three times over - Arrival, Blade Runner 2049 and Prisoners have all been shown - and this is where all three strands meet: the patience of Arrival, the sand-and-neon melancholy of 2049, and the dread of Prisoners, applied to the science-fiction novel most people had declared unfilmable. Villeneuve and cinematographer Greig Fraser shot on real sand in Jordan and Abu Dhabi with massive practical sets, so the heat and the scale are physical rather than rendered, and the ornithopters and spice harvesters were built rather than painted. Hans Zimmer's score throws out the orchestra for bagpipes, electric cello and processed human voices, which is why the film sounds like a religious ritual instead of an adventure. It won six Oscars, all of them for craft. The first hour is deliberately slow and political; the point is to make you understand a world before the war arrives. This is the setup - Part Two (8.4, also on your list) is the payoff, and it is waiting for a future round the moment you have seen where it starts.
